Short explanation for the non-neurologically-inclined:

  • you have a number of specific areas in your brain that light up when you hear specific human vocalizations, such as "aa", "eh", "ih", "sh", "dh", and so on

  • every such vocalization that corresponds to activity in a specific brain area is called a "phoneme" - another way to think about phonemes is as the smallest unit of human speech

  • your brain is wired for different phonemes depending on what language you acquired first - which is why Japs have trouble perceiving the difference between "R" and "L", Westerners struggle to differentiate between the Semitic "Hē" and "H̱et" and Arabs can't distinguish between "P" and "B"

  • David Moses and his team wrote software that reads and analyzes the output from the phoneme areas in your brain

  • they sat down their participants in a brain scanner, played them ten predetermined spoken sentences over headphones in a randomized order, and had their software analyze the brain activation of the participant

  • by looking at the phoneme area activation, the software was able to correctly identify which one of the ten predetermined sentences was being played to the participant in 90% of all cases

Key takeaways:
-> They didn't read their participants thoughts, they read their participants brain activation in response to hearing human-spoken sentences
-> In practice, this means you cannot use this technique to extract someone's 'inner voice' or thoughts
-> But it may be ridiculously useful for stroke or trauma patients who have difficulty in perceiving, processing or producing speech
-> This doesn't mean that things that are effectively equivalent to what you guys imagine as "mind-reading machines" aren't being developed - it's just that this particular study isn't actually related to that field
